uncited: Compositing and Output Generation defines the final stage of direct volume ray casting, where discrete volumetric samples are aggregated into a 2D image pixel [S1, S2, S10].
It solves the problem of optical integration, determining how light emitted or scattered by volume elements is attenuated by absorption and combined with background light [S1, S2].

This family is distinct from [Projection and MIP Techniques](6305-projection-and-mip-techniques.md) because it explicitly tracks opacity and transmittance for alpha blending, preserving depth cues, whereas MIP methods discard opacity for order-independent extremum aggregation [S1, S2, S10].

It differs from [Volume Raycasting Output Generation](4277-volume-raycasting-output-generation.md) by focusing on the mathematical accumulation logic itself, while the sibling article covers the broader implementation pipeline including ray traversal and transfer function sampling [S1, S2].
All methods in this family operate on a sequence of samples $(c_i, \alpha_i)$ encountered along a ray, where $c_i$ is the sample color (RGB) and $\alpha_i$ is the sample opacity (A) [S1, S2].
The core mechanism involves an accumulator state $(C_{acc}, \alpha_{acc})$ initialized to $(0, 0)$ (or background color/opacity) and updated iteratively for each sample [S1, S2].
The standard optical model assumes that light is emitted or scattered by the volume and attenuated by absorption [S1].
The term $(1 - \alpha_{acc}^{(i-1)})$ represents the transmittance, i.e., the fraction of light reaching sample $i$ from the camera side [S1, S51].
The final pixel color is often composited over a background color $C_{bg}$ using $C_{final} = C_{acc} + (1 - \alpha_{acc}) C_{bg}$ [S1, S14].
Early ray termination is a common optimization where the loop breaks if $\alpha_{acc}$ exceeds a threshold (e.g., 1.0), as further samples contribute negligibly to the color [S10, S12].
The front-to-back compositing equation is a standard result in volume rendering, derived from the Beer-Lambert law for light attenuation [S12, S43, S50].
Early ray termination was introduced as an optimization to reduce computational cost by skipping samples behind opaque regions [S10, S12].
MIP techniques originated in medical imaging to visualize high-density structures like bones without the occlusion caused by soft tissue [S1, S2].
